sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Suillus granulatus is a ringless bolete. Its cap is usually 4–12 cm wide, convex then flattening; the smooth, separable skin is sticky in wet weather and ranges from ochre or yellowish brown to reddish brown. Beneath the cap, short tubes end in small, round pores that are pale at first and then yellow. Young specimens may exude cloudy whitish to milky droplets from the pores; these can turn brown as they dry.

sections.title: Stem, flesh and spores
sections.text: The cylindrical stem is generally 4–8 cm long and has no veil or ring. It is pale to yellow, becoming yellower near the top, and bears pinkish-brown to reddish-brown glandular granules, especially near the apex. The whitish to pale-yellow flesh changes little when cut; smell and taste are mild or indistinct. The spore print is cinnamon-brown to yellowish brown.

sections.title: Habitat and lookalikes
sections.text: This species forms mycorrhizae with pines and grows on the ground, singly or in groups. Droplets on young pores, the granular stem and the lack of a ring help distinguish it from Suillus luteus, which has a ring and usually lacks these droplets. Features vary with age and region; a photograph alone cannot confirm a foraged specimen.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: Recommendations differ between countries. Anses recorded 25 poisonings linked to eating this species in France between July 1999 and March 2015, mainly digestive, sometimes with neuropsychological symptoms; it considers the species capable of causing poisoning even after canning, with no specific treatment established to eliminate the risk. DGfM includes it in its edible-mushroom list after sufficient cooking; the VAPKO list also includes it and advises removing the cap skin. These recommendations differ from the French health assessment and do not establish that it is risk-free.

traits: Cap 4–12 cm, convex then flattening, smooth and sticky in wet weather, ochre to reddish brown
Short tubes; small, round pores, pale then yellow, sometimes beaded with milky droplets when young
Pale to yellow stem, 4–8 cm long, dotted with pinkish-brown to rusty glandular granules, without a ring
Whitish to pale-yellow flesh, little change when cut; mild or indistinct smell and taste
On the ground beneath pines, singly or in groups
safetyNote: Anses reports 25 poisonings linked to Suillus granulatus in France between 1999 and 2015 and states that no treatment has been established to eliminate the risk. Some foreign mycological lists nevertheless classify it as edible under preparation conditions. If symptoms occur after eating a wild mushroom, contact a poison centre or emergency services immediately.
